summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed and remanded a termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the county failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the conditions producing the neglect could not be substantially corrected or eliminated so as to allow the child's safe return.
key_cases.relevance: It is a leading published Virginia example of appellate reversal for insufficient evidence supporting the agency's termination case, including scrutiny of the parent's language and cultural barriers.
key_cases.quote: Upon this evidence we conclude that there was no clear and convincing showing made of the statutory criteria required to support an order terminating residual parental rights.

key_cases.case_name: C.S. v. Virginia Beach Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed, vacated and remanded a termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that the evidence fell short of clear and convincing proof that the mother had failed to remedy substantially the conditions leading to foster care placement.
key_cases.relevance: It is a published Virginia reversal of an agency-driven termination where the Court found nothing in the record supporting the trial court's conclusions, including an agency concern rooted in the mother's distrust of government.
key_cases.quote: the evidence falls short of the standard of clear and convincing proof that mother did not remedy substantially the conditions which led to the child's foster care placement

key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed dismissal of a founded sexual abuse complaint, holding that the local department's failure to tape record the child victim's interview, absent any specific determination that recording was impractical or inappropriate under 22 VAC 40-705-80(B)(1), violated required procedure and was not harmless error.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Virginia example of a court setting aside an agency finding for failure to observe required investigative procedure.
key_cases.quote: It was essential, therefore, for the hearing officer to have access to the precise substance of S.J.’s statements.

key_cases.case_name: Commissioner, Virginia Department of Social Services v. Fulton
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed a circuit court that had converted a founded disposition to unfounded and purged the registry, holding that under the Administrative Process Act the reviewing court may reject agency factfinding only if a reasonable mind would necessarily reach a different conclusion, and may not reweigh witness credibility.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the limit of judicial reversal of agency findings: disagreement with the agency's credibility determinations is not enough.
key_cases.quote: It is not the trial court’s role to determine the credibility of the witnesses.

key_cases.case_name: Walker v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed and remanded because the circuit court wrongly placed the burden on the parents: an appeal from the juvenile court is tried de novo, only final orders are appealable, and on a § 16.1-283 termination petition the Department must carry the clear-and-convincing burden in the circuit court.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Virginia case reversing a lower court for misallocating the burden of proof on appeal from the juvenile court, and for treating a non-final interlocutory order as binding.
key_cases.quote: such a trial de novo in the circuit court grants to a litigant every advantage which would have been his had the case been tried originally in such court

timeline_requirements.deadline: 10 days to note an appeal to the circuit court, heard de novo
